title: Judicial Renaissance -- Ch. 18: Central Bank Employees Association v. Monetary Board: Constitutionality of Increases in CB Employees' Compensation
keywords: Central Bank Employees Association v. Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas
coequal and coordinate branches of government
primary_topics: Chapter 18 of 'Judicial Renaissance' -- CJP's account of Central Bank Employees Association v. Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas, in which the Court, voting 9 to 4, held that an initially valid provision of law can become subsequently unconstitutional when its continued operation would violate the equal protection of the law, and struck down the last proviso of Section 15(c), Article II of RA 7653 as an 'invidious discrimination' against the 2,994 rank-and-file employees of the BSP.

The majority's doctrine of relative constitutionality, expounded by ponente Justice Reynato S. Puno, under which a statute valid at one time can become void at another because of altered circumstances or changed conditions, applied here through a two-tiered scrutiny that let the proviso pass the 'rational basis test' but fail the 'strict scrutiny test' once seven other GFI charters exempted their rank-and-file from the SSL.

CJP's own dissent: that voiding the proviso was uncalled for, untimely and imprudent, that relative constitutionality was inapplicable and lacked express basis in positive law, that a becoming respect for Congress required leaving the alleged inequity to legislative cure, and that the provision passes the three-tiered standard of review for equal protection.

The companion dissents of Justice Antonio T. Carpio (the majority 'enacted' a pending bill and wrongly lumped the regulatory BSP with commercial, non-regulatory GFIs) and of Madame Justice Conchita Carpio Morales (a 145-page opinion attacking the ponencia's 'double standard,' its reading of GFI employment as the decisive trait, and its trespass on the congressional power of appropriation).
sub_topics: The holding stated at the outset: an initially valid provision of law can become subsequently unconstitutional when its continued operation would violate the equal protection of the law.

The facts: RA 7653 of July 3, 1993 abolished the old Central Bank and created the BSP; almost eight years later the Central Bank (now BSP) Employees Association, Inc. filed a petition for prohibition against the BSP and the Office of the President.

The challenged classification: officers (SG-20 and above) exempted from the Salary Standardization Law versus rank-and-file (SG-19 and below) who were not, which petitioners called arbitrary, capricious and not germane to the law's purpose of professionalism and excellence at all levels.

The respondents' side: the BSP argued the proviso could stand if read in harmony with the BSP's fiscal and administrative autonomy and the Monetary Board's mandate, while the Office of the Solicitor General argued the classification rested on actual and real differentiation.

The sole issue and the 9-to-4 ruling: the proviso was not infirm on its face, but subsequent laws amending the charters of seven other GFIs had worked a discriminatory effect, so its continued operation violated equal protection.

Relative constitutionality explained by Justice Puno with US cases and Rutter v. Esteban, and the two-tiered scrutiny -- the proviso passed the rational basis test because the officers' exemption addressed the BSP's lack of competitiveness in attracting competent executives.

Under strict scrutiny the disparity failed: no characteristics peculiar to the rank-and-file of the seven GFIs justified an exemption denied to those of the BSP, and a distinction resting on salary grade or officer-employee status is akin to one based on economic class and status, hence suspect.

The majority's caveat that judicial restraint and the rational basis test are the norm, but scrutiny must be stricter when the challenge is premised on the denial of a fundamental right or the perpetuation of prejudice against persons given special constitutional protection.

CJP's first ground of dissent: relative constitutionality is relevant only when the factual situation covered by the assailed law changes, and the American cases cited involved emergency-type police-power measures, while Rutter v. Esteban involved a remedial measure with a suspension period -- since the reason for the law still continued, the law itself must continue.

CJP's second ground: a becoming respect for Congress as a coequal and coordinate branch required giving it ample opportunity to legislate a cure, there was no urgency and no injury requiring immediate judicial action, and the Court has neither the authority nor the competence to create or amend laws.

CJP's third ground: the proviso passes the three-tiered standard of review because salary grade, class of position and government employment are not fundamental rights and non-exempt government employees are not a suspect class, and a law does not become invalid because of simple inequality.

The Carpio dissent: the majority did not annul a law but 'enacted' a pending bill, invading the legislative domain, and wrongly classed the regulatory BSP and PDIC -- funded by mandatory government exactions and facing no private competitors -- with commercial GFIs such as the LBP, SSS, GSIS, DBP, SBGFC and HGC.

The Morales dissent: the ponencia improperly combined the rational basis and strict scrutiny standards as a 'double standard,' when the persons and rights asserted remained the same and the US Federal Court had never applied more than one standard to a given set of facts.

Morales on in pari materia and on legislative intent: the SSL, the New Central Bank Act and the amended GOCC/GFI charters should be read together, and legislative records show exemptions were granted for institution-specific reasons -- proprietary character, direct competition with the private sector, and difficulty filling or retaining competent personnel -- not for mere GFI employment.

Morales's closing: with House Bill 123 pending in the Thirteenth Congress to exempt all BSP positions, judicial restraint was not merely preferable but mandatory, lest the Court substitute its policy judgments for those of the legislature, in whom the 'power of the purse' was constitutionally lodged.

notable_anecdotes: CJP records his own dissent from the 9-to-4 majority, opening it with the flat judgment that it would be 'uncalled for, untimely and imprudent' for the Court to void the proviso.

He notes that he did a close reading of the American cases cited in the ponencia and found that every law voided there for 'altered circumstances' had been an emergency-type measure passed under the police power.

He observes that Congress was in fact then deliberating amendments to the assailed proviso, with House Bill 123 pending in the Thirteenth Congress to exempt all BSP positions from the SSL -- the very relief the Court granted by decision.

He flags the sheer scale of Madame Justice Conchita Carpio Morales's Dissenting Opinion, 145 pages long, and reports its argument that the US Federal Court had never applied more than one standard of scrutiny to a single set of facts.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 18 of 'Judicial Renaissance' recounts Central Bank Employees Association v. Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas, which Panganiban opens with its holding: an initially valid provision of law can become subsequently unconstitutional when its continued operation would violate the equal protection of the law. RA 7653 of July 3, 1993 abolished the old Central Bank and created the BSP; almost eight years later the employees association sought to stop the implementation of the last proviso of Section 15(c), Article II, which exempted officers at Salary Grade 20 and above from the Salary Standardization Law while leaving the rank-and-file covered. The BSP answered that the proviso must be read with the bank's fiscal and administrative autonomy and the Monetary Board's mandate, and the Solicitor General argued the classification rested on actual and real differentiation. Voting 9 to 4 through ponente Justice Reynato S. Puno, the Court held the proviso was not infirm on its face, but that later laws exempting the rank-and-file of seven other government financial institutions had worked an 'invidious discrimination' against the BSP's 2,994 rank-and-file employees. Puno invoked relative constitutionality, citing US cases and Rutter v. Esteban, and applied a two-tiered scrutiny: the proviso passed the rational basis test, since the officers' exemption addressed the BSP's lack of competitiveness, but failed strict scrutiny because a classification by salary grade is akin to one based on economic class. Panganiban dissented, arguing that relative constitutionality was inapplicable and had no express basis in positive law, that respect for Congress as a coequal branch and the absence of urgency counseled restraint, and that the proviso satisfies the three-tiered review because neither salary grade nor government employment is a fundamental right or suspect class. He reports Justice Carpio's dissent that the majority had effectively enacted a pending bill and had wrongly lumped the regulatory BSP with commercial GFIs, and Justice Carpio Morales's 145-page dissent attacking the ponencia's 'double standard,' urging that the statutes be read in pari materia, and concluding that with House Bill 123 pending, judicial restraint was mandatory.
